kaigo-atomic-standing-cane.heading: Support for standing and the cane-walking sequence
paragraphs: Before helping someone stand, check how they feel and which movements they can make, explain what you will do and obtain consent. In the source’s hemiplegia example, the person sits slightly forward on the seat, draws the unaffected foot back and leans the upper body forward to begin standing. The principle is to move the center of gravity into a supported area and make it easier to bear weight on the unaffected side.

In this example, the care worker stands on the affected side and provides support to prevent the affected knee from buckling and the person from falling. Knee buckling means that the knee bends because it cannot support the body during standing or walking. After a major change in body or head position, check for dizziness, how the person feels and any change in their condition.

Three-action cane walking separates the sequence into ‘cane, affected foot, unaffected foot.’ Two-action walking combines ‘cane and affected foot, then unaffected foot.’ The source presents three-action walking as the more stable example. However, do not change the number of actions for speed alone without assessing the person’s abilities, equipment and actual walking.

In the example of assisted walking with hemiplegia, the care worker stands behind the affected side and supports the upper body or waist as needed. Connect the example of stepping with the affected foot first to its reason: the unaffected side supports the body as walking begins. Follow the individual plan and practical training for the specific support method and amount of assistance.

The example sequence for going up a step is ‘cane, unaffected foot, affected foot’; for going down it is ‘cane, affected foot, unaffected foot.’ The care worker is shown on a lower step than the person, behind them when going up and in front when going down. The position one step below describes the conditions in that diagram. Check the method against the handrail, step, cane and person’s abilities.

Remembering only the feet—‘unaffected side first when going up’—does not explain where the cane or helper goes. This text teaches how to understand the sequence and its reasons; it is not an instruction manual for trying unfamiliar assistance. Do not force the illustrated position on someone whose weight-bearing ability or joint condition is unsuitable. If the person feels unwell or you cannot provide adequate support, avoid forcing the action and seek assistance or a professional’s assessment.

kaigo-atomic-wheelchair-transfer.heading: Separate transfer preparation and execution from wheelchair movement
paragraphs: Transferring from a bed to a wheelchair and pushing the wheelchair after the person is seated are separate actions. Check the person’s condition, required number of helpers, what the person can do, equipment and method; explain and obtain consent. Do not record that the transfer is complete merely because wheelchair preparation is complete.

In the source’s hemiplegia example, the wheelchair is placed on the unaffected side and its brakes are applied while stationary. Check in advance the support the unaffected hand will use and the assistance needed to prevent the affected knee from buckling. Also check the wheelchair and floor. Positioning alone does not establish that everything is safe.

The source illustrates holding the far arm support with the unaffected hand, moving the upper body forward to stand, turning toward the wheelchair and sitting down. Standing, turning and sitting each require support suited to the person’s abilities and method. This is not an instruction to decide on your own to stand or pivot someone who cannot bear weight.

In the source’s transfer example, the person sits well back in the wheelchair, their feet are supported on the foot supports, and their feelings and condition are then checked. In practice, check the sitting depth suited to the person and wheelchair, body support, foot position, hands and clothing. Do not treat sitting down as completion: connect observations such as comfort and sliding to the care plan.

Before pushing the wheelchair, check whether the feet can rest on the foot supports and whether hands or clothing could become caught in the wheels. The source example places the unaffected hand on the arm support and the affected hand inside it. Check this example against the posture the person can maintain and the equipment’s conditions.

Before setting off, tell the person that the wheelchair will move, release the brakes using the checked procedure and then move. Also check the brakes for stopping, surroundings and the person’s condition. Actual transfers and wheelchair movement must follow the individual plan, wheelchair instructions and training. Do not treat a stage that has not happened as completed.

kaigo-atomic-wheelchair-curb.heading: Read direction and sequence in step and slope diagrams
paragraphs: Stop before a step and explain to the person what will happen. In the source’s upward example, the worker places a foot on the tipping lever and moves the push handles diagonally downward to raise the front. Read the illustrated sequence as gently placing the front wheels on the step and then raising the rear wheels.

The downward example is backward. The diagram shows the rear wheels being lowered slowly first, followed by controlled lowering of the front wheels after the rear wheels clear the step. It also shows the worker pressing the tipping lever with a foot and pulling the push handles diagonally downward to control the wheelchair’s tilt. The front/rear wheel order differs from going up. This explains how to read the source diagram; actual operation requires checking the equipment, route and person’s conditions and following a trained method.

For a steep downward slope, the source illustrates moving backward to prevent the person from sliding forward off the seat. The care worker checks safety behind them and adopts a supporting stance with one foot ahead of the other. Check whether the route can actually be used and which method is appropriate, considering the wheelchair type, slope, and helpers’ strength and number.

Distinguish the direction of force shown by the arrows, the wheelchair’s travel direction and the front/rear wheel sequence. Raising the front wheels and deciding when to lower them into contact are separate matters. Lowering is also illustrated as slow and controlled; the diagram does not mean that more force makes every step passable.

This is a reading of diagrams under the source’s conditions, not an instruction to teach yourself by trying them with someone in the wheelchair. Do not use foot supports as steps or force the wheelchair over unsuitable steps or slopes. Follow the plan and practical training for the actual route, equipment and assistance method, and check with the person responsible if anything is unclear.

kaigo-atomic-swallow-stages.heading: Five phases of eating and swallowing
paragraphs: Meals provide energy and nutrients that sustain bodily activity and life. They also offer enjoyment of flavor, daily rhythm and connection with other people. The presence of food in front of someone does not establish that their body has taken in the nutrients it needs.

In the anticipatory phase before eating, the person recognizes food through its color and shape, smell and other cues, and saliva secretion is prepared. The brain is involved in hunger and the wish to eat. This stage does not mean that food has already entered the stomach.

During the preparatory phase, food in the mouth is chewed and mixed with saliva to form a bolus: a cohesive mass of food ready for swallowing. In the following oral phase, the tongue mainly moves the bolus toward the throat. Distinguish chewing from moving food out of the mouth.

During the pharyngeal phase, the swallowing reflex occurs and the bolus passes through the pharynx. Rather than treating the epiglottis as an isolated lid, understand this as the stage in which coordination of the larynx and associated muscles protects the airway while moving food into the esophagus.

During the esophageal phase, the bolus travels through the esophagus to the stomach. Difficulty in any of the anticipatory, preparatory, oral, pharyngeal or esophageal phases may affect safe eating. Observing that someone chewed or that their throat moved does not confirm all stages or airway safety.

Eating connects movement to the eating area, maintaining posture, recognizing dishes, holding utensils, bringing food to the mouth, chewing and swallowing. Do not take over everything because one part is difficult. Consider separately what the person can do and which support they need.

Appearance and smell help the person recognize dishes, taste identifies flavors, and touch contributes to understanding mouthfeel and texture. Recognizing or liking a dish is separate from checking swallowing function. Follow the individual assessment and plan, and report observed changes to professionals.

kaigo-atomic-food-devices.heading: Distinguish purposes of food textures, posture and assistive items
paragraphs: Chopping, pureeing and softening food while retaining its shape are different modifications. Distinguish liquids from thickened liquids too. Follow the assessment of chewing and swallowing abilities and the individual plan; descriptions such as finely chopped, soft or liquid do not by themselves establish safety.

The source’s seated example shows sitting well back with the soles supported, leaning the upper body slightly forward and positioning the chin tucked down. The example of risk when the chin is raised also prompts a check of the helper’s position. This does not instruct everyone to adopt an identical position: follow the upper-body, head and chin positions assessed for the individual.

For eating in bed, check the individual method for supporting the upper body and head. The source illustrates supporting the body again after raising the backrest and returning it to the bedding; learn this in connection with reducing displacement and pressure. Actual movements must follow a trained method suited to the person. A side-lying example places the unaffected side down and supports the head with a pillow, but do not choose lying direction or posture from a diagnosis alone.

Posture diagrams are examples for understanding support. Do not independently pull or lift the person to reproduce an illustrated shape. Follow equipment instructions, the assessed method and practical training. Maintaining a posture alone also does not prove swallowing safety.

Spoons and forks with easy-grip handles and retaining straps support holding utensils. Angled spoons and forks are shaped so they can be used in a direction that makes bringing food to the mouth easier. Spring-assisted chopsticks help the pinching action. Observe how the person holds things and what is difficult, and use the selected utensils.

Easy-scoop plates help gather and pick up food; non-slip mats help keep items stable on the table. Easy-to-hold bowls and handled cups support holding containers. Assistive items serve different purposes, so check which parts the person can perform independently.

Being able to hold a cup tells you about hand movements. It is not evidence that the consistency of the drink matches the swallowing plan. Check equipment fit, food suitability and posture separately.

Consider the enjoyment of hot and cold foods, while still checking the temperatures the person will touch or eat. Do not prioritize keeping food hot above everything else. Check the temperature and food texture against the person’s sensations and plan, and do not independently add water or thickener.

kaigo-atomic-meal-checks.heading: Checks before meals, between mouthfuls and afterward
paragraphs: Before a meal, check the person’s condition, explain the support and obtain consent. Check that the meal is intended for them and compare its texture, treatment-related restrictions and allergies with the information already confirmed. Clean hands and place the tray where the person can understand its location. The source illustrates the helper diagonally in front on the dominant-hand or unaffected side.

Moistening the mouth before eating may be part of the plan. The source includes tea and soup as examples, but this is not an instruction to give thin liquids to everyone. Follow the person’s assessment and plan for drink consistency and method; workers must not give drinks to test swallowing function.

Adapt both the amount in each mouthful and the interval before the next to the person. Do not make shortening the meal the sole goal. Observe posture, speed, utensil use, chewing, swallowing and wishes. Do not add another mouthful while the person is still dealing with the previous one.

The helper sits at a height and position where they can see the person’s expression and mouth without making the person look upward. In its hemiplegia example, the source shows assistance from the unaffected corner of the mouth and withdrawing the spoon horizontally. Learn why pulling food upward could make the person extend their neck; actual operation must follow the individual method and training.

Discuss the menu and the person’s wishes at a suitable time when they can speak. To help prevent aspiration, avoid speaking to them while they are chewing and wait until they can talk. Respect wishes to rest or finish; remaining food is not a reason to force the person to continue eating.

Check with the person that the meal is finished, check for food remaining in the mouth and provide oral care suited to them. An empty plate alone does not establish who ate how much, whether the mouth is empty or whether nutritional needs were adequately met.

The source introduces remaining seated for about 30 minutes after eating as one example of a consideration for preventing aspiration pneumonia. Follow the person’s condition and plan for the actual resting posture and time; a uniform number does not replace assessment. Do not automatically move straight to lying down after meals. Provide support using the checked method.

Clock-position descriptions for someone with limited sight use directions from that person’s viewpoint. Twelve o’clock is the far side, six the near side, three the right and nine the left; other numbers indicate directions between these. Clock numbers describe positions here, not eating times or food amounts.

Explain not only dish names and positions but also heat, cold and seasoning. Check whether the person finds this method understandable, and tell them again if a dish is moved. If eating is unsuitable for their condition or they feel unwell, do not force assistance to continue. Follow facility procedures to seek assistance or a professional’s assessment.

kaigo-atomic-skin-structure.heading: Skin layers, sweat glands and care of skin folds
paragraphs: In a skin cross-section, distinguish the outer epidermis, the dermis beneath it and the deeper subcutaneous fatty tissue. Hair roots, sebaceous glands and sweat glands are not all lined up on the surface. Do not confuse their anatomical locations with sweat or dirt on the surface itself.

Hair grows from the portion within the hair follicle, and sebaceous glands secrete sebum. Ducts lead from the coiled sweat glands shown in cross-section to the skin surface, where sweat emerges. Read the structure by distinguishing glands, ducts and sweat on the surface; the diagram does not diagnose gland condition from the skin’s appearance. Sebum and sweat also help maintain the skin surface, but that does not mean secretions should remain on it indefinitely.

Eccrine sweat glands are widely distributed and contribute to heat loss through sweating. Apocrine sweat glands occur in areas such as the armpits. Odor is not determined by the gland’s name alone; it also involves factors such as the breakdown of secretions by skin bacteria.

Skin cushions external impacts to protect internal organs and protects the body from irritation by harmful substances. It also contributes to sensing stimuli and regulating body temperature. Rubbing hard to remove dirt may injure the skin you are trying to protect. Consider both cleanliness and maintaining the skin’s condition.

Moisture and dirt can remain in wrinkles and skin folds. Clean these areas gently according to their condition and remove moisture without rubbing. Although sweat helps release heat, that does not mean skin folds should stay damp for a long time.

The number of washes alone does not show the outcome of care. Check cleanliness, dryness, redness, skin damage and the person’s pain or discomfort. Report changes specifically, and adapt methods to the person’s condition and support plan.

objectives: Explain the sequences and reasons for support in the standing, cane-walking and step examples.
Check condition, equipment and training requirements rather than assuming a remembered sequence suits the person.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-standing-cane.prompt: Does ‘lead with the unaffected foot when going up a step’ fully explain the source’s cane-walking example?
options: Mentioning the unaffected foot also explains the sequence for placing the cane.
No. The cane sequence, helper’s position, and conditions relating to the person and equipment are also needed.
The statement also indicates whether the helper stands in front of or behind the person.
Knowing the upward foot sequence means the person’s abilities and the step conditions have already been checked.
rationales: The order of the unaffected foot does not supply the separate information about when to place the cane.
Remembering the foot sequence alone leaves out the cane, helper and environment, so it does not establish the complete method.
The statement does not describe the helper’s position. Do not infer it from information about the person’s feet.
Remembering the source sequence and checking whether the method suits the person and actual step are separate matters.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-wheelchair-tran.prompt: After only applying the brakes and positioning the wheelchair, someone wrote ‘transfer complete.’ What needs to be corrected?
options: Adding that the brakes were applied leaves the recorded ‘transfer complete’ stage unchanged.
Record that positioning the wheelchair also confirms the person’s turning direction and posture after sitting.
Because the brakes were checked, the transfer-complete record includes the person’s feelings after transfer.
Record that preparation is complete, and separately record only what has been confirmed about the actual transfer and the person’s condition after sitting.
rationales: More detail about preparation does not justify recording the unconfirmed result of the person actually transferring as complete.
This extends an equipment-position check to a transfer and post-transfer posture that have not been checked.
Brake condition and the person’s feelings after transfer are separate checks. Preparation alone provides no result about those feelings.
Wheelchair preparation, the person’s transfer, and their condition and posture afterward are separate stages. Do not record an outcome that has not happened as complete.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-wheelchair-curb.prompt: Why can the diagrams not be read as ‘handle the front wheels first, using the same sequence both up and down a step’?
options: Both use the tipping lever, so only the helper’s standing position differs.
The diagonal downward arrow at the handles prevents comparison of the wheel-contact sequence.
The sequence for placing or lowering the wheels differs between the forward upward example and the backward downward example.
‘Backward’ in the downward diagram refers only to the helper’s feet, separately from the wheelchair’s travel direction.
rationales: Using the same component does not explain differences in travel direction and wheel-contact sequence between going up and down.
The direction of force indicated by an arrow and the wheel sequence are separate information. The movements of the front and rear wheels can each be read.
The upward example places the front wheels on the step first; the backward downward example lowers the rear wheels first. Read travel direction together with the contact sequence.
Backward in the source describes moving the wheelchair backward down the step, not merely the helper’s foot direction.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-swallow-stages.prompt: Does being able to chew food alone confirm that the person swallowed safely?
options: No. The preparatory phase is followed by the oral, pharyngeal and esophageal phases; airway protection and other functions require separate checks.
Yes. Being able to chew shows that the pharyngeal phase also ended normally.
Yes. Forming a bolus and protecting the airway are the same check.
Yes. Observing chewing also includes the result of food passing through the esophagus to the stomach.
rationales: Successful chewing provides information about one stage, not every subsequent passage or the airway’s condition.
Chewing provides information about the preparatory phase. It does not establish passage through the pharyngeal phase or the outcome of airway protection.
Bringing food together and protecting the airway during passage through the pharynx are related but distinct functions.
Observing chewing alone does not confirm subsequent passage through the esophagus.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-food-devices.prompt: Do a non-slip mat and an angled spoon address the same difficulty?
options: Yes. Both only help the direction of scooping food and bringing it to the mouth.
No, but differences in the person’s grip strength alone are enough to choose between them.
No, but selecting an item by name completes the check of whether it helps the person eat.
No. The mat stabilizes items on the table; the angled spoon helps the direction of movement toward the mouth. Choose according to the person’s movements.
rationales: A non-slip mat stabilizes items on the table; it does not support the same direction of movement as an angled spoon.
Factors also include a sliding plate and the range through which the arm can bring food toward the mouth. Grip strength alone does not distinguish the two purposes.
Selecting equipment and checking actual comfort and the movements the person can make are separate stages.
This distinguishes the movements supported rather than just equipment names, and makes choices that use the person’s abilities.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-meal-checks.prompt: Does an empty dish alone confirm that the person ate enough and has no food left in their mouth?
options: An empty dish completes the intake check; only the mouth check remains.
No. Separately check the intake actually established, food remaining in the mouth and the person’s condition.
Observing an empty dish includes how the person ate and how much they ate.
An empty dish also confirms that the person wishes to finish the meal.
rationales: Why the dish became empty and who ate how much require separate checks. The amount cannot be treated as confirmed.
An empty dish is one observation, not evidence of every outcome concerning intake, the mouth and nutritional adequacy.
The dish’s condition at the time of observation and the preceding course of intake are separate information. Do not supply a course of events that was not observed.
The person’s wish to finish is information to ask about and confirm. Their words or intentions cannot be established from the dish alone.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-skin-structure.prompt: Should skin folds be rubbed hard every time to keep them clean?
options: No. Clean gently according to skin condition, remove moisture and check for redness and pain.
If the number of wipes is the same, the effect on the skin can be considered the same regardless of rubbing force.
Once visible dirt is gone, the absence of redness and pain has also been confirmed.
Because sweat releases heat, dampness in skin folds does not need to be checked separately from cleanliness.
rationales: Removing dirt is not an appropriate outcome if the skin is injured. Check both cleanliness and preservation of skin condition.
The number alone does not establish friction force or the person’s skin condition, so it does not establish an equal burden on the skin.
Removal of dirt, absence of skin injury and absence of pain each require separate checks.
Heat loss does not remove the effects of moisture remaining in skin folds. Check both cleanliness and dryness.
